sanskrit:
तस्मान्नार्हा वयं हन्तुं धार्तराष्ट्रान्स्वबान्धवान्।
स्वजनं हि कथं हत्वा सुखिनः स्याम माधव।।
image_english: It is not proper to kill our own kinsmen. How can we be happy after destroying our family?
caption:
Chapter 1, Verse 37

Arjuna asks a fundamental rhetorical question: ‘tasmān nārhā vayaṁ hantum’ (Therefore, it is not befitting for us to kill). He argues that while the Kauravas might be aggressors, they are still ‘svabandhavam’ (our own kinsmen). In the Vedic worldview, killing one’s family is a sin that negates any material gain. Arjuna asks, ‘sukhināḥ syāma mādhava’ (How can we be happy, O Madhava?). By using the name Madhava (Husband of the Goddess of Fortune), he implies that Kṛṣṇa should grant fortune, but this act seems to lead only to misfortune. Arjuna believes that happiness is derived from the social structure of the family. If the family is destroyed, the enjoyer of the wealth is gone, and thus the wealth itself becomes bitter. He is trapped in the bodily concept of life, thinking that his happiness depends on the physical presence of his relatives, rather than on the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord or the performance of duty.
